stories.text: In 1873 Horatio Spafford, a Chicago lawyer, sent his wife Anna and their four daughters ahead of him to Europe. Their ship, the Ville du Havre, sank after a collision in the Atlantic, and all four girls were lost. Anna cabled him two words: "Saved alone." Sailing out to join her, Spafford passed near the place where his daughters had died, and wrote these lines. Philip Bliss gave them their tune and named it after the ship.

John Newton spent his youth at sea and became the captain of slave ships. A violent storm in 1748 turned him towards God, though it was years before he left the trade. He became a minister in the village of Olney and wrote this hymn for his New Year's sermon in 1773. Late in life he spoke out against the slave trade he had once served.

Reginald Heber wrote this hymn for Trinity Sunday while he was a vicar in Shropshire. He later became Bishop of Calcutta and died in India in 1826; his widow published his hymns the year after. John Bacchus Dykes wrote its tune in 1861 and named it Nicaea, after the council that set out the doctrine of the Trinity.

Henry Francis Lyte was the minister of a fishing village, Brixham in Devon, for over twenty years. In 1847, ill with tuberculosis and about to travel south for his health, he preached his last sermon and, the family remembered, gave them this hymn that evening. He died in Nice a few weeks later.

Martin Luther wrote this hymn around 1529, drawing on Psalm 46: "God is our refuge and strength." It became the anthem of the Reformation, sung by people who had staked everything on the words of Scripture.

Fanny Crosby lost her sight as a baby and went on to write thousands of hymns. In 1873 her friend Phoebe Knapp played her a new melody and asked what it said. Crosby answered at once: "Blessed assurance, Jesus is mine!"

Joseph Scriven left Ireland for Canada as a young man and lived simply, helping people who could not pay. He wrote this poem to comfort his mother back in Ireland, never meaning it to be published. It was found, the story goes, when a friend sitting with him in an illness saw it by his bed.

Charlotte Elliott was an invalid for much of her life. In 1834, while her family were busy raising money for a school, she lay awake feeling useless and unsure of her faith. She wrote down the simple answer she had been given years before: come to Christ just as you are.

Isaac Watts did not write this as a Christmas carol. It is his version of Psalm 98, published in 1719, about the Lord coming to rule the earth. It looks forward to Christ's return as much as back to Bethlehem, which is why it is sung at Christmas and in between.

Isaac Watts wrote this in 1707 to be sung at the Lord's Supper. It is often called the finest hymn in English; Charles Wesley is said to have remarked that he would give up all his own hymns to have written it.

Joseph Mohr, a young priest in Austria, wrote the words in 1816. On Christmas Eve 1818, in the village of Oberndorf, he asked the schoolteacher Franz Gruber to set them for two voices and guitar. They sang it together at the end of the midnight service.

Joachim Neander, a German teacher and preacher, wrote this hymn of praise in 1680, the year he died at thirty. He loved to walk and pray in a valley near Düsseldorf that was later named after him, the Neanderthal. Catherine Winkworth translated it into English in 1863.

Francis of Assisi wrote his Canticle of the Sun near the end of his life, around 1225, calling on brother sun and sister moon, wind and water to praise their Maker. William Draper made this English version in the early 1900s for a children's festival in Yorkshire.

Robert Robinson wrote this hymn in 1758, when he was about twenty-two, a few years after hearing George Whitefield preach. "Here I raise my Ebenezer" comes from 1 Samuel 7:12, where Samuel sets up a stone and calls it Ebenezer: "Hitherto hath the Lord helped us."

The words come from an Irish poem many centuries old. Mary Byrne translated it into English prose in 1905, and Eleanor Hull put it into verse a few years later. Its tune, Slane, is an Irish folk melody named after the hill where, tradition says, St Patrick lit an Easter fire.
Wayne Hooper wrote this hymn for the 1962 General Conference session of the Seventh-day Adventist Church. It has been the church's theme song ever since.

Annie R. Smith worked with James and Ellen White on the Review and Herald in its first years, and wrote many of the early Advent believers' hymns. She died of tuberculosis in 1855, aged only twenty-seven. Her brother Uriah Smith became a leader of the young church.

Annie Hawks was a mother in Brooklyn, busy with her housework one morning in 1872, when she was struck by how much she needed Christ every hour of the day. She wrote the verses down, and her pastor, Robert Lowry, added the refrain and the tune.
Christopher Wordsworth, a nephew of the poet William Wordsworth, wrote this Sabbath hymn for his collection The Holy Year in 1862. It greets the day of rest as a gift and a foretaste of heaven.

John Newton wrote this hymn for the close of the week, and it was published in Olney Hymns in 1779. It welcomes the day of rest after the week's work, which is why it is often sung as the Sabbath begins.

Charles Wesley wrote this in 1739 to mark the first anniversary of his conversion. Its opening line is said to come from a friend, Peter Böhler, who told him that if he had a thousand tongues, he would praise Christ with them all.

Sabine Baring-Gould wrote this in a single evening in 1865, for children marching from one Yorkshire village to the next for a Whitsun festival. Arthur Sullivan, of Gilbert and Sullivan, wrote the tune it is sung to today.

William Whiting wrote this hymn in 1860; it is said he wrote it for a student who was about to sail to America and was afraid of the sea. It became known as the Navy Hymn, sung by sailors and those who wait for them at home.
Robert Lowry wrote words and music on a hot summer day in 1864 in Brooklyn, thinking of the river of life in Revelation 22 that flows from the throne of God.

writers.name: Fanny J. Crosby
writers.text: Blind from the age of six weeks, Fanny Crosby wrote more than 8,000 hymns, often several in a day, under her own name and dozens of others. She spent much of her life serving in New York's rescue missions.

writers.name: Isaac Watts
writers.text: Called the father of English hymns, Isaac Watts found the psalms of his day dull to sing and set out to write better ones as a young man. More hymns in this book are his than anyone else's.

writers.name: Charles Wesley
writers.text: Brother of John Wesley and a founder of Methodism, Charles Wesley wrote over 6,000 hymns. Many of them, such as "And Can It Be?", tell the story of his own conversion in 1738.

writers.name: F. E. Belden
writers.text: Franklin Belden, a nephew of Ellen G. White, wrote and composed many of the Adventist church's own hymns and edited its early hymnbooks, including Christ in Song.

writers.name: Annie R. Smith
writers.text: One of the first Adventist hymn writers. She worked on the church's paper with James and Ellen White and, in a short life, wrote hymns of hope that are still sung.

writers.name: Frances Ridley Havergal
writers.text: An English poet and gifted singer who knew much of the Bible by heart. She wrote "Take My Life and Let It Be" in 1874, after a night of prayer for the people in the house where she was staying.

writers.name: John Newton
writers.text: A slave-ship captain turned minister, John Newton wrote the Olney Hymns with his friend the poet William Cowper, and later worked with William Wilberforce to end the slave trade.
